summary:
Colima is a state of Mexico, and a trans visitor's exposure there is set by Mexico's national framework rather than by any Colima statute identified in the sources reviewed. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised anywhere in the country, and same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction. Nothing in the inventory indicates that Colima has enacted a measure targeting trans presence.

Legal gender recognition is settled state by state. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that as of March 2025, 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two further states operate one in practice without having enacted it, six legislatures have enacted nothing at all, and only seven states extend recognition to children. The Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors in 2022, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure.

Where no procedure exists the consequences are concrete. Human Rights Watch documents identity-document mismatch driving discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with recorded incidents in Guanajuato and Tabasco. The Human Rights Watch and Community Center for Inclusion report of 6 March 2024, examining Tabasco, a state with no recognition procedure, found that without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and excludes trans people from employment, health services, education and financial transactions.

Lethality governs the national picture. More than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished in 2022, and impunity for transfemicide is thought to run higher still. Only two of the 32 states have created the offence: Nayarit was the first, with penalties up to 60 years, and Mexico City followed in July 2024 with the Paola Buenrostro law, punishable by up to 70 years.

Killings continued through the period reviewed. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.
tangentialFactors:
Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP, published 22 November 2024, concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice. The analysis cautions explicitly that it must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months.

The transfemicide statute in Mexico City takes its name from Paola Buenrostro, a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished; activists describe the law as critical to their sense of safety. Two of 32 states criminalising the offence marks an emerging but still marginal legislative trend.

The Tabasco evidence supplies a comparison point for what an absent state procedure produces: the same reporting period records the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gómez in Villahermosa, alongside document-driven exclusion.
localsOnly:
Residents of Colima stand, as residents of a Mexican state, under the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation's binding guidelines on legal gender recognition issued in 2022, which also extended the right to minors; only seven of the 32 states extend recognition to children in practice, so availability for minors varies sharply by state.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible recognition procedure, which sets the standard national authorities are held to.

Where recognition is delayed or refused, residents carry documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care, education and dealings with police.

Same-sex marriage has been available nationwide since 2009, and homicide impunity above 95% as of 2022 is a resident-facing condition of the criminal justice system.
outOfScopeNotes:
Colima's specific standing within the national count is unresolved: the inventory does not state whether Colima has enacted an administrative recognition procedure, operates one in practice without enactment, or belongs to the six legislatures that have enacted nothing. No Colima statute on legal gender recognition is quoted or dated in the sources reviewed.

Whether Colima's penal code recognises transfemicide as an offence, and at what penalty, is not sourced here; the two documented statutes belong to Nayarit and Mexico City.

No Colima-specific enforcement data, documented incidents of violence against trans people, or local police and hospital practice appear in the inventory. The incidents cited are from Guanajuato, Tabasco and Mexico City.

The sources do not identify which procedure a visitor presenting documents issued elsewhere would encounter in Colima, nor whether Colima recognises gender markers changed in another state.
